segs.text: Module two, objective two. Two key parameters, volume of distribution and clearance. The apparent volume of distribution, V D, is the volume the amount of drug in the body would have to dissolve in to give the concentration measured in plasma. It is not a real body space, which is why it is called apparent. It is a proportionality constant between the amount of drug in the body and the plasma concentration. So V D equals D B, the amount in the body, divided by C p, the plasma concentration at the same time. For a bolus, the amount in the body at time zero is the dose, so V D also equals D zero over C zero, which finds V D from a dose and an initial concentration.

card.m: V<sub>D</sub>: apparent volume, not a real body space

segs.text: A drug that leaves the blood for the tissues has a low plasma concentration, and so a large V D. A drug held in the blood, for example by binding to plasma proteins, has a small V D. V D is given in liters, in liters per kilogram, or as a percent of body weight. For a percent, one liter is taken as equal to one kilogram. So ten percent of an eighty kilogram patient is eight liters. She said, in kinetics, our body weight is always in kilograms.

card.m: leaves blood for tissues → low C<sub>p</sub> → large V<sub>D</sub>
held in blood, protein bound → small V<sub>D</sub>
percent of body weight: 1 L = 1 kg

segs.text: Her lecture example puts the same one hundred milligram dose into three different volumes of distribution. The relation is the same one rearranged: C zero equals D zero divided by V D. With a V D of one liter, one hundred milligrams over one liter gives one hundred milligrams per liter. With ten liters, one hundred milligrams over ten liters gives ten milligrams per liter. With one hundred liters, one hundred milligrams over one hundred liters gives one milligram per liter. Milligrams divided by liters leaves milligrams per liter each time. The amount of drug is the same, but these would be three different drugs, and the larger the V D, the lower the plasma concentration.

Clearance, Cl T, is the volume of plasma cleared of drug per unit time. It measures elimination without saying how the drug is removed. It is also called drug, systemic or total body clearance. Clearance equals k times V D, where k is the elimination rate constant in per hour and V D is in liters. Per hour times liters leaves liters per hour, the unit a clearance must have. This line is not on the equation sheet. She said, I want you to take this one with you to your grave along with the half-life equation.

card.m: Cl: volume of plasma cleared of drug per unit time

segs.text: The second form is Cl T equals D zero divided by A U C from zero to infinity, the area under the plasma concentration time curve. Use it when a dose and an A U C are given instead of k and V D. Milligrams divided by milligram hours per liter leaves liters per hour. On the equation sheet it is written Cl T equals F D zero over A U C, where F, the fraction absorbed, is one for I V. Clearance is useful for two reasons: it stays constant, and it links the dose directly to the area under the curve. Clearance and V D are both constants for a given drug in a given patient, so changing the dose or the concentration does not change them.

card.m: Cl and V<sub>D</sub>: constant in a given patient

segs.text: Her questions test that constancy. One asks which value increases when the I V bolus dose increases. Only the plasma concentration does; clearance, half-life and V D stay the same. At the end of calculation problems she asks what doubling the dose does to the half-life, the clearance and the initial concentration: no change, no change, doubled. A true or false item says that clearance increases as concentration increases. That is false, because clearance is a constant.

card.m: dose ↑ → C<sub>p</sub> ↑; Cl, t½, V<sub>D</sub> unchanged
dose × 2: t½ same, Cl same, C<sub>0</sub> × 2

segs.text: A single best answer poll asks which parameter describes elimination as volume of fluid cleared of drug per unit time. The answer is clearance, not biotransformation, elimination rate or excretion. In calculations the usual trap is the unit of V D. It can arrive per kilogram, such as three liters per kilogram, as a percent of body weight, as liters, or not at all, to be found as dose divided by C zero. A percent or per kilogram V D must be multiplied by the weight in kilograms, and the answer is in liters, not kilograms. From the fish tank model of clearance, the part she uses is that only free, unbound drug can be cleared, and protein bound drug cannot.

card.m: V<sub>D</sub>: L/kg, % body weight, L, or {{frac:D<sub>0</sub>|C<sub>0</sub>}}
L/kg or % × weight in kg → L
